strengths: Provides a coherent, well-motivated diagnosis that optimization landscape issues, not just estimator statistical quality, are the dominant bottleneck for OPL in large action spaces — an angle largely underexplored relative to the extensive estimator-centric literature.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: closed-form oracle policies are derived for nearly every major IPS-based estimator (IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, PC), unifying disparate methods under one analytic framework and clarifying their inductive biases.

Formal optimization-theoretic results (plateau length and exponential local maxima scaling with effective action-space size Keff) are proven with explicit constructions, and are used constructively to motivate 'objective-aware parametrization,' giving a principled explanation for why POTEC outperforms OffCEM despite sharing the same oracle.

Proves concavity (strong concavity with L2 regularization) of PWLL objectives for linear-softmax policies and derives convergence guarantees (O(1/√T) and geometric rates), giving formal grounding to the empirically observed stability.

Extensive empirical validation across three genuinely large-scale action spaces (60K, 200K, 1M items), with systematic hyperparameter sweeps (batch size, LR schedule) and numerous appendix ablations (seeds, reward noise, cluster count, logging support size, smaller K, pessimism-based regularization) that consistently support the central claims.

Honest and precise positioning: the paper explicitly disclaims algorithmic novelty for PWLL (crediting existing offline-RL BC-style objectives) and clearly delineates limitations (no OPE/model-selection use, loss of concavity guarantee for deep end-to-end training, dependency of oracle on logging policy coverage).
weaknesses: The central optimization-friendly objective (PWLL/weighted log-likelihood) is not new — it is essentially reward/advantage-weighted behavioral cloning already used in offline RL (AWR, CRR, etc.) and even in the bandit literature (LPI, BPR); the paper's novelty rests mainly on repackaging/diagnosis rather than a new method, which somewhat limits its scientific contribution beyond an empirical/theoretical audit.

The formal concavity guarantee (Proposition 3.1) and the associated convergence theory hold only for linear-softmax policies; for the more practically relevant end-to-end deep parametrizations, the argument in Remark 3.2 is purely heuristic (analogy to cross-entropy gradients) and is not empirically validated with deep architectures in the experiments.

The reward model used in experiments is a simple deterministic/binary indicator derived from held-out user history, which may not capture the more complex or noisy reward distributions found in real recommendation systems; the noise ablation (Appendix E.4) only partially addresses this via synthetic Bernoulli corruption.

PWLL's oracle policy is inherently coupled to the logging policy π0 (e.g., π*_LPI ∝ r·π0), meaning its 'competitive or superior' performance may be partly an artifact of the specific (SVD top-k, near-deterministic) logging policy used throughout; broader stress tests with more diverse/adversarial logging policies (e.g., far more uniform or adversarially deficient) would strengthen external validity claims.

While extensive sweeps are shown, the paper does not report formal statistical significance tests (e.g., confidence intervals or hypothesis tests across the batch-size/LR grid) to support the claim that PWLL 'often outperforms' IPS-based objectives, relying instead on qualitative visual comparison of curves and shaded bands.

The claim that optimization dominates estimation is demonstrated primarily via a proxy (higher/lower validation reward under sweeps and lower MSE-reward correlation), but a more direct causal test (e.g., controlling for identical initialization/optimizer while varying only the objective's concavity properties in a fully matched setting) is only shown in the toy 3-action illustration, not at the large-K scale.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored question in OPL: whether optimization difficulty, rather than estimator statistical quality, is the binding constraint in large action spaces. This is a useful reframing of a widely-used estimator-centric paradigm.

Strong theoretical contribution: closed-form oracle policies are derived for a comprehensive set of IPS-based estimators (IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, PC), with rigorous proofs in the appendix. This unifies disparate methods under a common analytical lens and clarifies what each estimator's implicit inductive bias actually is.

Formal optimization-pathology results (Propositions 2.1/2.2 on plateaus and exponential local maxima) with explicit problem-instance constructions, plus a concavity/strong-concavity result for PWLL objectives and accompanying SGD convergence guarantees (Appendix D), give the empirical claims a solid theoretical grounding rather than relying purely on intuition.

Extensive, large-scale empirical evaluation on three real recommendation datasets spanning 60k to 1M actions, with systematic sweeps over batch size, learning-rate schedule, and clustering granularity, plus a large number of appendix ablations (seeds, reward noise, hyperparameter sensitivity, smaller action spaces, pessimism, logging-support size) that collectively provide fairly comprehensive support for the central claim.

The paper is transparent about limitations (PWLL is not usable for OPE/policy selection, concavity only holds for linear-softmax, oracle policies depend on logging-policy coverage) and clearly positions PWLL as a known technique (reward-weighted BC/AWR) rather than overclaiming novelty.
weaknesses: The core proposed remedy (PWLL) is explicitly not new -- it is reward/advantage-weighted behavioral cloning borrowed from offline RL. The paper's contribution is therefore largely diagnostic/empirical rather than methodological, which somewhat limits its originality even though the framing is useful.

A very standard and widely used variance-reduction/optimization-stabilization technique -- self-normalized IPS (SNIPS) -- is mentioned only in related work but is absent from the main empirical comparisons in Section 4, despite being a natural, simple baseline that specifically targets the kind of ill-conditioning the paper attributes to non-concavity. Its omission weakens the claim that IPS-based objectives are inherently and unavoidably hard to optimize relative to alternatives already in common use.

Main empirical results (Figures 2, 3, and 4) do not report variance/error bars across seeds, even though seed variability is later shown (Appendix E.3) to be substantial for IPS-based methods; this makes the headline comparisons in the main text harder to assess statistically, and the more careful seed-averaged results are relegated to the appendix.

The evaluation reward is constructed semi-synthetically (binary reward from held-out user interactions, with a logging policy built from SVD embeddings and temperature/top-k truncation chosen by the authors), which is reasonable but means the 'ground truth' policy value used to judge OPL success is itself an artifact of the experimental design rather than a truly independent measure; this should be discussed more explicitly as a source of potential bias in the comparison.

No wall-clock/compute cost comparison is provided despite 'trainability' being the central claim; some IPS-based methods (e.g., DR, OffCEM, POTEC) require auxiliary reward models or clustering, and it would strengthen the paper to know whether PWLL's practical advantage also holds when compute/tuning budgets are equalized rather than just compared via reward vs. hyperparameter sweeps.

The theoretical plateau/local-maxima propositions are proved via specific adversarial problem instances (Lemma C.3 constructions) rather than showing this is typical/generic behavior; while the empirical results support the qualitative conclusion, the theory alone establishes existence of bad cases rather than characterizing how often or how severely this occurs in realistic problems.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored gap: the paper convincingly argues and demonstrates that optimization landscape, not just estimator statistical properties, is a dominant factor in the success of off-policy learning (OPL) in large action spaces (up to 1M actions).

Strong theoretical grounding: closed-form oracle policies are derived for essentially all major IPS-based estimators (IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, PC), giving a unifying and clarifying view of their implicit biases; propositions on optimization plateaus and exponential local maxima are rigorously proven (with explicit problem-instance constructions in the appendix), and PWLL's concavity for linear-softmax policies is formally established along with SGD convergence guarantees.

Extensive, well-designed empirical evaluation across three large-scale real datasets (MovieLens 60k, Twitch 200k, GoodReads 1M) with controlled optimization sweeps (batch size, LR schedule, seeds) that directly test the central hypothesis, plus a rich set of ablations in the appendix (reward noise, cluster count sensitivity, logging support size, smaller K regimes, pessimism baselines) that consistently support the main claims.

Actionable, practically useful guidance for practitioners (objective-aware parametrization; prefer PWLL-style objectives for optimization robustness), clearly distinguishing this diagnostic/compatibility contribution from claims of new estimator novelty, which is an honest and clear positioning.

The reinterpretation of POTEC as an optimization strategy for OffCEM (rather than a new estimator) is an elegant and insightful observation, supported by both theory (same oracle policy) and experiments (consistent performance gap explained purely by parametrization).
weaknesses: The headline theoretical results (plateau length and exponential local maxima) are existence results built on carefully constructed problem instances (Lemma C.3) rather than showing these pathologies are typical/generic across problem distributions, which somewhat limits the strength of the claim that this explains real-world optimization difficulty at scale.

PWLL itself is explicitly not a novel method (directly ported from offline-RL advantage-weighted regression/behavior cloning), so the paper's contribution is primarily diagnostic/empirical rather than methodological; readers seeking a new algorithm may find the core recipe (log-likelihood weighting) fairly well-trodden.

A significant practical limitation, acknowledged by the authors, is that PWLL cannot serve as an OPE estimator or be used for policy selection among candidates, which restricts its applicability in the many real-world pipelines that require both learning and reliable evaluation/selection.

The reward signal in the main experiments is a binary hidden-item indicator, a simplified proxy for real-world rewards; while an ablation with synthetic noise is included, it would strengthen the paper to test with more realistic, continuous, or multi-valued reward distributions.

Absolute value differences between methods in the main results (Figure 2) are sometimes modest and are not accompanied by variance/error bars in that figure (though seed-based variance analysis is relegated to the appendix), making it harder to judge statistical significance from the main text alone.

The illustrative toy landscape (Figure 1) uses only 3 actions and 2 free parameters, which is a helpful visualization but a very simplified proxy for the claimed exponential-in-K difficulties in actual million-action settings.
